data.title: Sri Lanka’s public data, brought together and explained
data.description: Public projects, transport, schools, hospitals and population data—starting with Sri Lanka.

content.headline: Put the country in view.
content.subheadline: Public projects, transport, schools, hospitals and population data—brought together, sourced and explained.

children.text: “Developing country” should describe a problem, not excuse it.

Sri Lanka is full of plans, promises and public spending. It is much harder to find one reliable account of what was planned, what it cost, who was responsible and what happened next. This project starts by putting that information in one place.

data.title: About
data.description: Why I am bringing Sri Lanka’s public-interest data together in one place.

content.headline: You cannot hold a government to account with data you cannot find.
content.subheadline: Developing Country is my project to put Sri Lanka’s public-interest data in one place—and write clearly about what it shows.

children.text: I live in Sri Lanka and previously lived in Hong Kong, where I saw what well-run urban development can do for daily life. Back home, “developing country” too often works as a shrug. Corruption, missing records and institutions that do not publish make it hard to establish what is happening, let alone what to fix.

This site is the groundwork. It brings together datasets on public projects, transport, schools, hospitals, population and more. Every dataset carries its source, its vintage, the date it was last checked and an honest account of its limits—including the gaps where usable data does not exist.

The long-term ambition is an independent think tank: analysis that asks why a policy is failing, what better urban development could look like and whether public promises were kept. That standing has to be earned through the work. For now, this is a personal project built in the open.

data.coverage_note: Coverage is uneven: some topics have official sources, some only community maps and some nothing at all. Where data is missing, we say so instead of filling the gap.

Which neighbourhoods sit beyond walking distance of a bus stop? Which announced projects have gone quiet? Where do schools and hospitals cluster, and where are they missing? Start with a question. data.title: Are 40% of Colombo’s housing complexes over 40 years old?
data.dek: News 1st reports a ministry claim about ageing housing. The original report is located, but the complete inventory needed to reproduce the percentage has not been found publicly.
data.claim_source_title: 40% Of Colombo Housing Complexes Over 40 Years Old
data.research_question: Can the reported 40% share of ageing Colombo housing complexes be independently reproduced?
data.methodology: Located the original News 1st report and compared its geographic scope and reference date with Parliament, NHDA and UDA publications. Reviewed the Treasury building-return template. No complete eligible-complex inventory was located; this tracks an external claim and does not present a verified percentage.

children.text: What was reported

News 1st’s 12 September 2026 report attributes a 40% share of housing complexes older than 40 years to the housing ministry. It separately attributes a count of 96 authority-managed apartment complexes within Colombo city limits to Deputy Minister T. B. Sarath. The article does not supply the list or explicitly establish the denominator used for the percentage.
What we can establish

The original article matches the Instagram screenshot. That establishes the source of the statement, not the underlying age distribution. NHDA and UDA publish dates for individual schemes. Parliament’s August 2025 report concerns 45 ageing projects in Colombo District, so it cannot independently verify a city-level percentage reported in September 2026.
What would verify it

Obtain the full eligible-complex inventory and the age calculation as of the claim’s reference date. Identify the number exceeding the age threshold and divide it by the eligible total using the publisher’s counting and rounding rules. Treat mixed-age blocks, reconstruction and uncertain dates explicitly. The 96-complex total must be confirmed as the denominator before using it.
Can this extend to other public buildings?

Yes, there is a concrete collection mechanism: Treasury’s 2023 building-return template includes construction year. A populated extract and coverage assessment are still needed. This is a related data gap; it does not verify the housing claim. A CoC issue date should remain distinct from a completion year, and building age alone does not establish structural condition.

data.editorial_notes: Review source links, claim scope and the distinction between reporting and independent verification. The exact News 1st article is linked. Both data-gap records and this claim are drafts; publish gaps first, then the reviewed claim. Missing-data references are resolved to CMS IDs by the seed importer.

children.text: What this dataset contains
This layer brings together 1,129 named places tagged as visitor attractions on OpenStreetMap. It includes cultural sites, landmarks and other places people have chosen to map for visitors.
How it is used here
Open the live map to see where those places cluster and where the map becomes thin. It can be combined with roads, population and other layers in the explorer.
What it cannot tell you

OpenStreetMap is built by contributors, so coverage varies from place to place. A blank area does not mean there is nothing to visit, and a mapped point does not tell us about quality, opening hours or accessibility.

How it is used here

The platform summarizes ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 into an approximately five-kilometre display grid. Each cell keeps the dominant class among deterministic samples, its official class code and a categorical vegetation grouping.
How it is used here

A dominant coarse-grid class hides smaller and mixed patches. WorldCover reports modeled categorical land cover—not NDVI, live greenness or current vegetation condition—and its global accuracy does not establish the accuracy of every local cell.

children.text: What this dataset contains

This layer stores 354 areas: for each of the 110 stops, each of the seven lines and the whole network, the area within a 5- and 10-minute walk along the mapped streets and paths, and the 800 m straight-line circle. Each area carries its estimated residents, schools and hospitals.
How it is used here

Compare the walking areas with the circles to see where rivers, rail lines and missing street links cut people off. About 510,000 residents live within a 10-minute walk of a stop, against 898,000 inside the circles.
What it cannot tell you

Residents are estimated by spreading each GN division’s Census 2024 population evenly over its area, and daytime workers and students are not counted. Walks follow OpenStreetMap streets and paths at 80 m a minute, ignore slope, crossings and footpath quality, and start from stop locations compiled by lk_metro.

children.text: What this dataset contains

This is the routing graph behind the Colombo walking-access analysis. It turns connected streets and footpaths from OpenStreetMap into a network that the platform can traverse from a stop or other starting point.
How it is used here
The graph is an input to walking catchments rather than a finished public indicator. Its most visible use is in the Metro Bus access layer, where routes are calculated along mapped connections.
What it cannot tell you

A routing graph cannot see pavement condition, lighting, traffic danger, steps, gates or temporary obstructions unless those details are mapped. Missing connections can materially change a result, so calculated access should not be mistaken for an on-the-ground accessibility audit.

One row per CM line and one network row. How it is used here

About 510,000 residents, 19.7% of the study area, live within a 10-minute walk of a stop; 800 m circles would claim 898,000. Population is spread evenly within each GN division, so homes clustered along roads are not modelled. Residents only: workers, students and visitors are not counted. Offices and businesses are Overture Maps listings, not jobs: no headcount or floor area, and coverage is uneven.

source_manifest.title: ESA WorldCover 2021 v200
source_manifest.licence: CC BY 4.0

children.text: What this dataset contains

The platform samples ESA WorldCover 2021 v200 onto an equal-area 100 metre grid, counts classified pixels inside each district and derives class area and share. Shares use classified district pixels as the denominator.
How it is used here
The chart ranks all 25 districts by tree-cover share. A second chart keeps Colombo District’s class mix. The table has every observed WorldCover class for each district.
What it cannot tell you

These are modeled, resampled estimates rather than field or cadastral measurements. WorldCover is categorical land cover, not NDVI or current vegetation condition, and the 2020 and 2021 products use different algorithms. Tree-cover share is not forest inventory and is not a ranking of the largest districts by area.
